claims.text: The initial material is a non-equilibrium, metastable solid-solution-containing Mg-based lightweight high-entropy alloy.
High-temperature exposure causes the metastable solid solution to decompose by thermally activated nucleation and growth of Mg-rich intermetallic compounds.
Mg-rich intermetallic compounds preferentially nucleate at grain boundaries and other microstructural heterogeneities.
Intermetallic phase separation changes local diffusion paths and elemental partitioning.
Intermetallic formation redistributes passivating elements such as Cr or Al when those elements are present.
The redistribution caused by intermetallic formation disrupts the kinetics, continuity, and integrity of the protective oxide scale.
Faster or more extensive intermetallic formation causes poorer corrosion and high-temperature oxidation resistance than in the initial metastable state.
In situ high-temperature XRD can reveal temperature-dependent phase transformations, new-phase formation, and oxide formation in real time.
The relevant high-temperature service regime extends from above 500 °C to approximately 1100 °C.
Air and controlled oxygen partial pressures are relevant environments for studying high-temperature oxidation.
Exposure to 3.5% NaCl solution or salt spray represents the relevant corrosive service regime for the proposed alloy.
The volume fraction of Mg-rich intermetallic phases will increase with exposure time and temperature.
Samples with more rapid or extensive intermetallic formation will develop a less continuous or more defective oxide scale.
Samples with more rapid or extensive intermetallic formation will exhibit higher corrosion current density and lower polarization resistance than the initial state.
High-temperature sintering can produce a Laves-associated intermetallic phase in a high-entropy alloy initially containing solid-solution phases.
Local composition and processing history may influence the transformation kinetics.

The hypothesis is falsified if no significant Mg-rich intermetallic nucleation or growth occurs during aging, or if intermetallic formation is not associated with measurable degradation relative to the baseline.
